## What to build

Pickup's Bump-class classifier (`git-loopy/python/git_loopy/bump_class_pickup.py`) must never write a Release-target label for an inferred `major`. When the classifier answers `major` for an issue that carries no `vX.Y.Z` label, Pickup writes no label and reports a distinct, named outcome: a major needs a human-applied label. Everything else stays as it is. A human-applied major-successor label (for example `v1.0.0` after `0.11.1`) is still honoured, and the existing `already_labelled` path never reclassifies it. Inferred `minor`/`patch`/`none` behave as before.

The rule applies in every repository git-loopy runs in. It exists because the Release target only ratchets upward: one ordinary issue misread as breaking would move the whole line to the next major's `alpha`, and only a by-exception operator commit could undo that.

Pickup classification is Python-only. The shell and PowerShell Orchestrators only advance from labels already present, so no other family member changes. Update `docs/releases/README.md` ("Advancing the target") and the `CONTEXT.md` **Bump class** / **Release target** entries to state the rule once it ships.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An unlabelled issue whose classifier proposal is `major` gets no label written, and the classification reports a new outcome (for example `major_needs_human_label`) through the existing diagnostic/report path.
- [ ] An issue already carrying a human-applied major-successor label (`v1.0.0` after `0.11.1`) is unchanged: it is not reclassified, and Integration advances the line to `1.0.0-alpha.N` as today.
- [ ] Inferred `minor`, `patch` and `none` produce the same labels as before (regression tests in `tests/test_bump_class_pickup.py`).
- [ ] When the line target is already a higher major (for example a `1.0.0-alpha` line), an inferred `major` still writes nothing new. An inferred minor/patch still ratchets to the current target, as today.
- [ ] `docs/releases/README.md` and `CONTEXT.md` describe the rule. The Python suite and `ruff check` on touched files pass.

## What to build

The PowerShell Orchestrator reaches the same verdict as the reference member on the same input. An operator runs `git-loopy.ps1` against a **Pool** whose head awaits a pull-request merge. They see that candidate passed over with the pull request named, and never spend a session discovering it. An all-waiting Pool ends as an **All-blocked Run**.

This is a port, not a redesign. #692 settles the decision and #695 proves it in the reference member. The PowerShell reading of it has five parts:

- The references are requested on the `gh issue list` call this port already makes, in the one place its shallow field set is named.
- The pull-request states are resolved in one `gh api graphql` request per read. This port has no such transport today.
- The verdict and its precedence are computed in PowerShell.
- The unbound-Pool rule and the **Pin** follow from the verdict.
- `wrapper.pickup.skipped` is emitted with the reason the reference member emits.

This port has no **Rolling dispatch**.

Port-local hazards to close rather than inherit:

- **Membership never refuses on its own.** Only a pull request read as open refuses.
- **A failed read decides nothing.** A failed state read, or an unreadable node, is `readiness_unprovable`. It is never a wait and never an admission.
- **An old gh fails loudly.** If gh cannot serve the field, the Run fails at preflight. A missing field is never read as "no pull requests".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The PowerShell port turns its **Owed waiver** on #692's Awaiting-merge fixture into a **Fixture claim**.
- [ ] Its Conformance suite drives its production readiness decision and unbound-Pool rule through every case.
- [ ] Against a stubbed `gh`, the suite proves that the references ride the collection read, and that the state read happens at most once per read and not at all when no candidate carries a reference.
- [ ] An Awaiting-merge candidate is passed over at **Pickup**, stays in the **Pool**, and charges no **Strike**.
- [ ] An Awaiting-merge **Pin** is passed over and spent.
- [ ] An all-waiting Pool ends `all_blocked`. Its diagnostic says the Pool waits on open blockers or on pull requests to merge, not on blockers alone.
- [ ] Any unprovable refusal ends the Run `preflight_failed`.
- [ ] Every candidate Blocked today reports exactly the reason it reports today.
- [ ] The PowerShell README describes the new skip.
- [ ] The PowerShell Orchestrator suites loop is green.

## What to build

An operator runs `git-loopy run` against a **Pool** whose head's work already sits on an open pull request. They see that candidate passed over at **Pickup**, and the skip names the pull request (`awaiting_pull_request_merge: owner/repo#N`). No session starts and no **Strike** is charged. If every refusal in the Pool is a wait, the Run ends at once as an **All-blocked Run**.

On 2026-09-26 this was #679, waiting on #688. Each of two Runs spent one or two sessions and a Strike on it. Both then ended `all_skipped`, an ending that tells the operator to repair labels.

This is the reference slice. It lands the transport, the verdict and the serial Pickup path together, and proves them at #690's Seam 2 and Seam 3.

- **The references.** The closing-pull-request references ride reads the IssueSource already makes: the collection read, and the serial Pickup's authoritative re-read.
- **The states.** The referenced pull requests' states are resolved in the single extra request per read that #692 settles, and in no request when no candidate carries a reference. There is never a round-trip per candidate.
- **A new transport.** No member calls `gh api graphql` today. The pull-request state read lands behind the GitHub client seam, so the fake client can drive it.
- **The decision.** The **Readiness** decision gains **Awaiting merge**, with the precedence #692 decides. #693 made the verdict the one place that states a refusal's reason and class. The serial admit, the unbound-Pool rule and the **Pin** all follow from the verdict.
- **Pull-request candidates.** This rule never refuses one.

Hazards this slice owns:

- **Membership is not state.** gh's `closedByPullRequestsReferences` keeps merged pull requests, omits closed-unmerged ones, and carries no state. No candidate may be refused on membership alone.
- **A failed read is not a wait.** A failed state read, or a node the token cannot see, is **Unresolved readiness**. It neither refuses the candidate as Awaiting merge nor admits it, and a Pool holding one ends `preflight_failed`.
- **The gh floor.** Confirm that the gh version the Runner already requires serves `closedByPullRequestsReferences` on both reads. Raise the floor if it does not. A gh that cannot serve the field fails loudly at preflight, and is never read as "no pull requests".
- **Nothing Blocked today changes.** A candidate with both an open blocker and an open pull request reports `blocked_by_open_dependency`, exactly as it does today.

**Shared file.** This ticket edits `git-loopy/python/git_loopy/loop.py`, at least for the serial all-blocked diagnostic, which today says every candidate waits on an open blocker. The #680 remediation is concurrently editing the Parallel-loop code in that file. Expect to rebase onto whichever of the two lands first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Seam 2.** IssueSource tests against the fake GitHub client prove that:
  - the references ride the collection read and the authoritative re-read;
  - the state read happens at most once per read, and not at all when no candidate carries a reference;
  - a failed state read, or an unreadable node, gives `readiness_unprovable`;
  - a gh that cannot serve the field fails loudly.
- [ ] Python turns its **Owed waiver** on #692's Awaiting-merge fixture into a **Fixture claim**. Its Conformance adapter drives the production Readiness decision and unbound-Pool rule through every case.
- [ ] An Awaiting-merge candidate:
  - is passed over at **Pickup**, with `wrapper.pickup.skipped` naming every open closing pull request, in connection order;
  - stays in the **Pool**, where the closure whitelist, the collection Event and the emptiness test still see it;
  - charges no **Strike** and starts no session;
  - becomes admissible again on the next Iteration once its pull request closes unmerged.
- [ ] An Awaiting-merge **Pin** is passed over and spent, like a Blocked Pin.
- [ ] A merged pull request does not refuse the open issue it references. A draft pull request does.
- [ ] A `ready-for-agent` pull-request candidate stays admissible while the issue it closes is Awaiting merge.
- [ ] The serial all-blocked diagnostic says the Pool waits on open blockers or on pull requests to merge, not on blockers alone.
- [ ] **Seam 3.** A serial-loop end-to-end regression, built from the minimised repro of the 2026-09-26 diagnosis, runs a Pool made of an Awaiting-merge head and a candidate Blocked by it. The Run ends `all_blocked` with zero agent sessions and zero Strikes, and its **Unbound-Run notice** names the pull request to merge. Prior art: the `all_blocked` tests in the iteration end-to-end suite.
- [ ] Every candidate Blocked today reports exactly the reason it reports today.
- [ ] The Python suite is green.

## What to build

An operator whose Run ends `all_blocked`, because its Pool waits on open pull requests, can see which pull requests to merge. The notice names them beside the blockers outside the Pool, and groups the Awaiting-merge candidates by the pull request each one waits on. Today the notice names only blockers. On 2026-09-26 the operator's next act was to merge #688, and nothing named it.

The **Unbound-Run notice** is presentation. It reads only the Event stream: the `wrapper.pickup.skipped` reasons, or the `refusals` recorded when a Rolling Run ends. So it needs only the reason that #692 decides, `awaiting_pull_request_merge: <owner/repo#N>[, …]`, and no change to how the Runner picks up work.

Python and the Rust **Dashboard** both claim `unbound-run-notice`. Their notices therefore land together, with the new cases, so neither suite is left red while the other catches up.

Hazards to close rather than inherit:

- **Blockers are found by prefix.** The notice finds blockers by stripping the `blocked_by_open_dependency` prefix. A reason with the new prefix must be read as the pull requests it names. It must never be dropped, and never misread as blockers.
- **Only blockers are tested against the Pool.** #690 names every pull request to merge, and applies the inside-or-outside-the-Pool test to blockers only. A pull request in another repository is named by its full reference.
- **Distinct rendering is assumed, not proven.** #690's user story 18 asks that the Dashboard show an Awaiting-merge skip distinctly from a Blocked one. The Dashboard prints a skip's reason verbatim today, so this may already hold. Prove it with a test.

**Shared surfaces.** The #680 remediation is also editing the Dashboard's README. Expect to rebase onto whichever of the two lands first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `unbound-run-notice` gains cases for an all-waiting Pool: one from a serial skip stream and one from a Rolling `refusals` record. Each names the pull requests to merge beside the blockers, and groups candidates by the pull request they wait on.
- [ ] The Python and Rust notices both pass the new cases and every existing case.
- [ ] The lines for a Pool that waits only on blockers are unchanged.

## What to build

When a **Lane contribution**'s session returns a captured outcome, whatever its disposition, the Python reference Orchestrator emits `wrapper.contribution.work_finished`. Each one is followed by exactly one of:
- `wrapper.integration.admitted`
- `wrapper.integration.parked`

A host failure (including a Checkpoint failure), a **Stop** before the session, and Run-exit reclamation never reach that boundary, so they emit only `wrapper.contribution.end`. A bare `unchanged_branch` end therefore tells a host failure apart from a session that produced nothing.

In the Rust Dashboard core, the Event:
- decodes to a typed payload;
- keeps dimming the Lane's **Activity window**;
- stops the row's Active timer, so a Parallel issue's Active time is its Lane work only (ADR-0065).

The row's **Status** stays unchanged until the Integration Statuses arrive in #682.

## What to build

`wrapper.pipeline.quiescent` leaves the Event vocabulary everywhere in the **Runner family**, and the rolling Conformance stream stops contradicting the Wrapper contract.

Every phase `wrapper.pipeline.quiescent` names is already announced by an Event with a producer:
- `wrapper.serial.requested`
- `wrapper.stop.requested`
- the serial **Iteration**'s own `wrapper.iteration.start`
- `wrapper.rolling.refill_turn`

Nothing reads it (ADR-0065). After this ticket, no Orchestrator catalogue, Conformance fixture or Wrapper-contract list names it.

Separately, two of the rolling stream case's three published contributions, c-0002 on #43 and c-0003 on #44, end without the `wrapper.auto_close` the contract requires: *"a publication whose runner-driven closure has not yet verified is not a contribution end."* Each gains one, so the order #675 pins can be checked against the fixture.

- [ ] The Dashboard-insights oracle's rolling case drops it. Every snapshot after its former position is re-indexed, with its expectations otherwise unchanged.
- [ ] The rolling stream case carries a closed `wrapper.auto_close`, stamped with the contribution identity, between `wrapper.integration.published` and `wrapper.contribution.end` for c-0002 and c-0003. The Python, shell and PowerShell round-trips and the Rust fold stay green.

- [ ] `event_schema_version` does not move for the removal (ADR-0046 precedent).
- [ ] Commentary in the Event catalogue and the scheduler that names the retired type is updated.
- [ ] The AGENTS.md feedback loops this touches are green: the Python suite, the Rust core, and the shell and PowerShell suites.
